paragraphs.text: Heaven rejoices when stars rise among stars, and harbors rejoice when small ships gleam among the great ones, and when clouds play upon clouds as they rise, and sprinkle and scatter dews of sweetness. The Church rejoices too, when peoples hasten after peoples and feasts press upon feasts at the holy places. They do not change their strength as the places change; rather, as the places change, they renew their affection: from blessings to blessings, from church to church. Or rather, to speak like the Apostle, "from faith to faith" and "from glory to glory"; and the prophetic word is fulfilled: "They shall go from strength to strength." Yesterday the royal crown of the apostles made us radiant, and today the wreath of the martyrs gives us light. The Church takes both the crown and the wreath, and in her the prophet's word is fulfilled: the Church is "a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of God." Let the labors of these witnesses crown our bosom, and let the light of the lamps crown the walls of this temple, as a wall and a rampart. A double rampart has been set around us by the Trinity, for nothing in heaven or on earth receives light without the Holy Trinity. These lamps resemble the pattern of the Creator [?]: what God does in secret, these lamps do openly. For this light has surrounded us like a rampart, just as he promises: "I will be a wall of fire around my people."

Truly the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord like many waters that cover the seas. And now, through the holy peoples, the hidden word of the prophet is fulfilled indeed: "The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness." The prophets proclaimed this, but they did not speak these words about the present state of things. Who would not know that the earth is the Lord's, and its fullness? Or who would doubt whether some other lord has a share in creation? For all of us, believers and unbelievers alike, plainly know from long custom that everything belongs to God. The prophets did not speak this about the present state of things, but about the first error, when idolatry set the earth ablaze, when people burned with zeal for images, when God was not known and those who were no gods received worship.

At that time, as the Apostle says, "they worshiped the creature and not the Creator." The holy prophets saw the earth as though some tyrant had driven it into exile, and they cried out to those who had gone astray: "The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness! Why do you wander in error? Why do you assign the regions of the earth to all sorts of gods?" For places were called by the names of the demons. Just as a rebel who breaks in by force makes another's kingdom his own, so the demons broke into the world and seized each part of it for themselves. Some were called gods of the Lycians, some of the Athenians, others of the [?], and others of the Achaeans. Each had parceled out its own region, and places were named after the god to whom they were dedicated. For example, the Athenians took their name from the goddess they worshiped, and the City of the Sun from its god, and every people from its own god. Not to lengthen the account with a list: places were named after the names of the gods.

So that you are not misled by this earlier account, pay attention to the Scripture that agrees with it. The ancients supposed that each of the gods had been allotted one region of the earth, and that God held the region of Judea. That is why the Assyrian said, when they came against the land of the Palestinians: "Have the gods of each land saved their own land, that the God of Israel should save you?" The ancients supposed that none of those reckoned as gods was Lord of all. Just as each of the falsely named gods had received his own land, so they thought God held the land of the Palestinians as his own possession. As another barbarian also said, he had power only over the mountains of the Palestinians. To those in error, then, who carved the earth away from the one lordship and counted the regions under heaven as belonging to many lordships, the prophets cried out: "The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness." Then, as if he were asked to show why the whole earth is the Lord's, he brings forward the evidence of creation to establish the bounds of his lordship: "He himself," he says, "founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers."

From then on the whole earth was filled with the glory of Christ, and the whole earth became full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah says, "like many waters that cover the seas." What nature does not allow, the law of faith brings about. You know, brothers, that many rivers from every region under heaven pour into the seas, yet they have not covered them; rather, they themselves were covered instead. But the new preaching promises a new kind of power. "The knowledge of God," he says, "has filled the earth like many waters that cover the seas." What cannot happen in nature, he establishes for knowledge. Just as it is impossible for the sea to be covered by outside waters, so it was impossible, by the ordinary course of things, for the earth to be filled with knowledge. Yet behold, the word spread out and filled all the ends of the earth, and the teaching of the gospel covered the seas. Which sea? The one in which people were tossed about as in an abyss. The word of God went forth and filled every region under heaven, and what Daniel said was fulfilled: the stone cut from the mountain without hands became a great mountain, and the whole earth was filled with it. Sometimes he compares the teaching to water covering everything under heaven, because the teaching moved swiftly on its course and the word filled the ends of the earth. At other times he compares it to a mountain, because of the loftiness of the teaching and because its speech about God reaches up to heaven. "In the last days," he says, "the mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest, and the house of God shall be above the tops of the mountains." Which house? The Church. It is not built on mountains; it stands firm in the loftiness of its speech about God. The Church is the house of God, as Paul writes to Timothy: "so that you may know," he says, "how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church." And why above the mountains? The Life-giver says: "A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden."

The stone was cut without hands because Christ was born without a man. The stone was cut without hands because Christ was born without the union of marriage. And the stone became a great mountain and filled everything under heaven. Someone might think this a forced interpretation and ask, "What does a stone have to do with one born in the flesh?" So I must show that human births are also called hewings from rock, which proves that being cut out means being born. The prophet Isaiah says to the people: "Look to the solid rock from which you were hewn." Then, to explain the rock, he adds: "Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you." Do you see that he calls human births hewings from rock?

And why does he say the people were born from a rock? Because Sarah was barren, and a rock is barren and bears no fruit. He calls her a rock because she was barren by nature, though she was made fruitful by grace. "Look," he says, "to the rock from which you were hewn." There the hewing of stone signifies the birth of the people; in the same way, here the stone cut without hands means Christ's birth in the flesh. And see how careful he is. Stones often split off and fall from mountains without hands, but he did not say "it split off" or "it broke away." He said "it was cut," because it was to signify the Lord's birth: "The stone was cut without hands." For he was not born by the laws of nature but by a new kind of birth-pangs. Untouched by marriage, the flower blossomed from a virgin womb, became a great mountain, and filled the earth. If the events did not match the words, this defense would be in vain, and we would be trying to force the truth with falsehood. But the events came before our words and cry out for themselves, and the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of Christ. If we are ungrateful for these benefits, we too will hear from the Lord: "Even if you are silent, the stones will cry out." A stone was cut without hands and became a great mountain, and all the peoples hasten to this mountain and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob."

Note carefully how he first presents the turning of the Gentiles, and only then the calling of the Jews. For first people from the Gentiles believed in Christ, and after them people from the Jews as well. "Many nations shall come and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and he will tell us his ways, and we will walk in them." And what does he add next? "For out of Zion," he says, "shall go forth the law." See how he presents the law of the second covenant, for the first law came not from Zion but from Mount Sinai. "Out of Zion," he says, "shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he shall judge among the nations," and the rest that follows, one point after another. Once he has foretold the turning of the Gentiles, the prophetic Spirit cries out to the Jews and says: "And now, O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord." Do you see? First the Gentiles believe, and then the Jewish people are called.

You have the type of Joseph. The types of the Life-giver were fulfilled in advance. Joseph first reigned in Egypt, and only afterwards over his ungrateful brothers. He reigned first over the Egyptians, who were foreigners, and afterwards over his brothers, who were his own kin. See how wonderful it is: is not what David said wholly fulfilled in Christ? "He set it as a testimony," he says, "in Joseph" — that is, a prophecy that would bear witness was placed in Joseph. If he had stayed at home with his father Jacob, Egypt would not have received its healer. Note this carefully: if Joseph had stayed there, pampered by his father, Egypt would not have received the provider who found the remedy for the famine. Joseph was sent to go and see his brothers and the flocks; the Only-begotten was sent into the world to seek the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Dreams adorned Joseph, and miracles glorified Christ. "I saw that I and my brothers were reaping, and their sheaves bowed down to my sheaf." Since the brothers would do him homage because of the threat of famine, God showed the outcome of the coming events beforehand through sheaves of grain, which are food. First the sheaves bowed down to him, because the brothers would be the first to bow down to him. First the famine drove them down to Egypt, and on their second visit they recognized their brother. The first time they stood before him trembling, as before a ruler; the second time they recognized him and were honored. They recognized him and were glorified as the brothers of Joseph in his glory.

The brothers hated Joseph because of his dreams. They did not realize that it was not him they hated but the One who showed him the dreams. Did he see the dream by his own will? So whoever fought against the dreamer was battling against God. But see how wickedness blinds. Why fight against the dreamer? Will the dreams come true, or will they prove false? If they come true, what scheme could you devise to stop the truth? And if they prove false, why be jealous of the ravings of a night-phantom? Joseph went to see his brothers, to do them a work of love, and they repaid kindness with ingratitude and insult. He spoke words of peace to them, and they banded together for a fight and battled against him, so that the Life-giver's word might be fulfilled: "They hated me without cause." See the wonder: "The dreamer is coming," they say. The vision of the dream terrified them, or rather not the vision itself but the suspicion that it would come to pass. They plotted death for the saint, and God turned their wickedness into a work of his providence. For it is God's work not only to bestow gifts from himself but also to turn our wickedness to good use. They wanted to kill their brother, and Reuben offered good counsel: "Let us not kill him, for he is our brother and our flesh; let us throw him into one of the pits." He had in mind how he might save him. But God was in fact carrying out the work of his providence. Joseph is not killed; he goes down alive into the pit, for he was a type of the Living One, who went down alive into hell. Joseph went down into the pit, and the pit was empty of water: a likeness of the Life-giver's tomb, which was empty of the dead.

Joseph was thrown into the pit. Judah, taking pity on his brother, proposed a fine plan so that he would not be killed in the pit: "What profit is there if we kill him? Come, let us sell him." Judah took care to spare his brother, but the all-knowing God was carrying out the work of his providence. It was fitting then for Joseph to be sold through Judah, for the sale of the Life-giver also came about through Judas the betrayer. The Ishmaelites took him and carried him off to Egypt. On what? On camels. And what were the camels carrying? Resin, balm and incense. It was fitting indeed that the sweet ointment of humility [?] should be sent along with incense. From the story itself one can see how wickedness unwillingly praised the merchandise to get a higher price. The Ishmaelites asked, "Is this boy any good?" The brothers were forced to comply, because they saw the silver in the buyers' hands. "He is freeborn," they say, "of good birth. He does not know how to steal; he is incapable of swearing falsely." Willing or not, wickedness showed itself to be a liar.

Joseph went down to Egypt, for the Life-giver too was to go into Egypt. Joseph was sold to foreigners; Christ was handed over to the Gentiles: "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of the Gentiles." Joseph was handed over to the Ishmaelites, and Jesus to the Gentiles. Joseph went down to Egypt and at first was afflicted, for at first Jesus too was not received by the Gentiles; later they worshiped the one they had persecuted and insulted. The type was truly portrayed when Joseph suffered at the hands of the lustful [?] woman. The woman seized hold of Joseph's garments, as death seized the Life-giver's body. Joseph slipped out of his garments and left them with the wanton woman, as the Life-giver, when he rose, left his garments in the tomb. Joseph enters the prison, for Christ too was to enter the tomb. Joseph was put in charge of the prisoners, for Christ too is King of the living and the dead.

See the nobility of his soul. Outwardly he was in prison and in chains; the free man was in slavery, and the one destined to be honored with kingship sat in prison. Yet he never wavered like someone of little faith. He did not say, "Where are the dreams now? Where are those false fantasies?" He did not say, "Where are the oracles of God that foretold my future? You promised me a kingdom, and I endure slavery. You promised to give me authority, and I do not even enjoy the freedom everyone has. I have gone down from freedom into slavery; I have gone from comfort into prison." No such thought entered his mind. He persevered and waited for things to come to pass. And who will testify that he expected these things to come to pass and did not waver? There were, it says, two servants of Pharaoh in the prison. They had dreams and were downcast. Joseph says to them, "Why are you downcast?" They answer, "We have had a dream, and there is no one to interpret it." He did not say, "Pay no attention to dreams; let my dreams be a lesson about the dreams of others." This shows that he was waiting for his own dreams to come to pass. "Tell me," he says, "and I will explain it to you." Have your own dreams been fulfilled, that you interpret other people's? He interprets the dreams, and he waits for his own dreams to be fulfilled. Note this carefully, and pass from the type to the truth. If you want to learn what Joseph was like, do not learn it from his brothers, for envy hides the truth and casts the free man into slavery. Nor from the Ishmaelites, for they bought the free man as a slave. Nor from his mistress, for she slandered him because of her shamelessness. If you want to understand what sort of person Joseph was, ask his father, and he will tell you: "a son, and a beloved son." Now come to Christ. If you want to understand who Christ is, do not learn it from the Jews, for envy veils the truth. Nor from the idolaters, for they hate the one who destroys their images. Nor from the heretics, for just as the Ishmaelites did not know that they had bought a free man, so the heretics do not recognize him, and so they make the free one a slave. Not from the Jews, for they are enemies of the cross; not from the idolaters, for they hate the one who exposes their idols; not from the heretics, for they are a type of Ishmael, who was born not of the free woman but of the slave woman. The Ishmaelites are a type of the heretics, and the sons of the free woman a type of the believers. When the patriarch blessed Joseph, he said: "Your blessing shall be from the dew of heaven and from the fatness of the earth." Note that these are God's gifts, given from heaven and from earth. These gifts were not given to Ishmael, for he did not have them: "By the sword," it says, "you shall live." The Ishmaelites have no other trade by which to make any gain except the sword. The heretics are like them: they believe neither the oracles of heaven nor the prophets, but take up the sword against them. And rightly so, for they are Ishmaelites: they live not by the word of God but by the sword of folly.

From now on, then, do not learn what Christ is like from the Jews, or the idolaters, or the heretics. If you want to understand, take your knowledge of him from his own root. See what the One who begot him testifies about him: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." The Father calls him Son, and you call him a creature? "This is," he says, "my beloved Son." And again: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son." Does the Father not persuade you? Do the oracles of the prophets not fill you with awe? Do the ranks of the apostles not shame you? Then let the demons put you to shame. You do not heed the Father, who says, "This is my beloved Son"; nor Paul, who proclaims, "You are the Son of the living God"; nor Isaiah, who calls him "mighty God." You have rejected the Scriptures; at least feel shame before the demons. Matthew says that demons came out of many people, crying out, "You are the Son of God." Mark likewise says that they submitted to his word and said, "We know who you are, the Son of God." Luke too declares that when the demons saw him, they fell down before him, crying out and saying, "We know who you are, the Son of God. Have you come [?] before the time to judge us?" The demons confess him as the Son of God, and you call him a creature? You stand in great danger, for you make the demons more righteous than yourself; a great heap of evils makes lesser evils look righteous. That is why he said to Jerusalem, because of the great heap of her evils, "Sodom has been justified more than you" — meaning that, beside your sins, the city of Sodom appeared righteous.

You have the type; now bow down before the truth. If Joseph had not gone into Egypt, the land of the Egyptians would have perished from famine. And if the Life-giver had not come into the world, the whole world would have perished from hunger for the divine word. To hear that God's divine word is food, listen: "Behold, I will send upon you not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord." What a wonder! How the type was portrayed beforehand in the prophet! You have seen the type in Joseph; now see in Daniel too the type of the resurrection. They threw Daniel into the pit against the will of Darius and Cyrus; Christ goes up onto the cross against the will of Pilate, who consented unwillingly. The agreement of the princes forced King Darius, and the agreement of the Jews forced Pilate. Darius hurried at dawn to look into the pit and see whether Daniel was safe; the apostles and the women hurried at dawn to the tomb to see whether the Living One was alive.

Turn, you heretics, from unbelief to faith; do not be worse than water. Water saw Jesus and became wine, while you say "Son" and call him "servant." He performed his first sign at Cana of Galilee, so that the word might be fulfilled which says: "Galilee of the Gentiles, the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light." The first sign took place at a wedding, because the human race first grows through marriage, and a wedding is the root of the human plant. He blesses the root in order to bless the branches. And here is what amazes me: not only that he was invited and agreed to go, but that he did not go to a wedding in some distinguished house; he went to the wedding of a poor man. The man whose wedding it was was poor, so poor that even the little wine he had ran out. He was poor in possessions, but he grew great in the treasures of truth.

The Lord appeared and changed the water into wine. His mother prompts him: "They have no wine," she says. She was his mother according to the flesh and his handmaid according to his Godhead. She was his handmaid according to his divine nature, and became his mother according to the dispensation. He was her God and her Son: God by his lordship, and Son by the dispensation. "They have no wine." "What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come." Some have understood this passage to mean that he was promising something of another kind [?]. But he reproaches his mother because she was still looking at the Lord of men as a mere man. He rebuked her not for prompting him but for prompting him as one would a man. Many have taken "my hour has not yet come" to mean "the time for signs has not yet come." But if it had not come, how could you perform the sign? No, he reproaches his mother for prompting him needlessly and before the time, since God has no need of being reminded. "The time of my manifestation has not yet come, for no one yet knows who I am." And so that you may learn that he did not say this to refuse the sign, but because she had prompted his power, note that his mother understood the honor and said: "Do whatever he tells you."

He spoke, and changed the water into wine — he who also turns water into oil. Through the olive tree he turns moisture into oil, through the stalk into wheat, through other plants into spices, and through trees into fruit. In everything he turns each plant to its own flavor: one rain, and flavors of every kind are produced. Do not marvel that he changed water into wine; marvel far more that throughout all creation he turns one rain into colors and flavors of every kind, and blood into milk, and all these again into their own colors and flavors. By daily habit people have come to disregard his great works, and only something new, from some unexpected act of his providence, seems marvelous. Otherwise, why do you not marvel at how he turns the blood in women's breasts into milk, white by nature? Why are you not astonished that he changes dark hair to white, which no dyer's skill can ever achieve? Dyeing white into black is possible, but making black white is utterly impossible. Blood cannot be dyed, and what has once been dyed red cannot be turned white. Yet he turns dark blood into white blood, and changes black hair into white hair, so that you may learn that it is not nature that brings this about; he is the one who set nature its law to be so.

So when you see him going to the wedding and turning the water into wine, marvel; but know that this is only a small taste of his great works. It is great, though not by the measure of the wonder-worker, but by the measure of the love with which we enjoy it. And now it is right and fitting to understand that the miracles of the Life-giver were very small by his own measure, but very great for those who enjoyed them. Moses bears witness that this is so when he recounted to them the wonders that were done in the land of the Egyptians: “Remember how the Lord your God brought you out of the land of the Egyptians with great signs and fearful deeds.” See how he marveled at the miracles. See also how the worker of the signs regards the deed as small: “All this I did to the Egyptians, so that you may tell your children’s children how I made sport of the Egyptians.” Do you see? What seem like miracles to us are play to God. But enough of this.

May the light of Christ dawn upon us, and may the divine Word enlighten our souls, so that we may strip off the works of darkness and put on the works of light, make the preaching shine with our words, and adorn with our deeds the promise that we have made; so that by words and deeds, by faith and by God’s good pleasure, we may send up glory to the all-holy Trinity forever. Amen.
